'''David Edmund Caro''' (29 June 1922 – 15 August 2011) was Australian [[physicist]] who was [[vice-chancellor]] of the [[University of Ballarat]], the [[University of Melbourne]] and the [[University of Tasmania]], interim vice-chancellor of the [[Northern Territory University]], and [[chancellor]] of the University of Ballarat. He was instrumental in creating [[UniSuper]], the [[superannuation]] scheme of university employees. He supported Antarctic research and travelled to Antarctica twice, paying a brief visit to the South Pole.

After service in the [[Royal Australian Air Force]] (RAAF) during [[World War II]], during which he maintained [[radar]] systems, he graduated from the University of Melbourne with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1946 and a [[Master of Science]] degree in 1949. He then went to the [[University of Birmingham]] in England, where he assisted the expatriate Australian professor of physics, [[Mark Oliphant]], in the construction of the Birmingham proton [[synchrotron]], which formed the basis of his 1951 [[Doctor of Philosophy]] thesis. He returned to the University of Melbourne, where he became head of the physics department in 1961 and deputy vice chancellor in 1972. Caro was vice-Chancellor of the University of Tasmania from 1978 to 1982, and of the University of Melbourne from 1982 to 1987.

==Early life and education==
[[File:Birmingham proton synchrotron 03 (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Completing the wiring of the second variable oscillator unit of the Birmingham proton synchrotron in 1950, with his plan drawings in front of him.]]
David Edmund Caro was born in [[St Kilda, Victoria]], on 29 June 1922,<ref name="NAA">{{cite web |title=Caro, David Edmund |via=RecordSearch |publisher= National Archives of Australia |url=https://recordsearch.naa.gov.au/SearchNRetrieve/Interface/ViewImage.aspx?B=5375533 |access-date=23 October 2025}}</ref> the only son of George Alfred and Alice Lilian Caro.<ref name="Wedding" /> He was educated at [[Geelong Grammar School]] and entered the [[University of Melbourne]] in 1940, intending to pursue a degree in science. His studies were interrupted by [[World War II]], and he enlisted in the [[Royal Australian Air Force]] (RAAF) on 20 September 1941. Like many recruits who knew some physics, he was sent to study radar systems. He was commissioned as a [[pilot officer]] on 9 March 1942, and was subsequently promoted to [[flying officer]] on 6 September 1942 and [[flight lieutenant]] on 1 December 1943. He served in the Northern Territory with [[No. 44 Wing RAAF|No. 44 Radar Wing]] and at [[Port Moresby]] in Papua, where he maintained radars in support of Nos [[No. 6 Squadron RAAF|6]], [[No. 7 Squadron RAAF|7]] and [[No. 100 Squadron RAAF|100]] Squadrons.<ref name="NAA"/><ref name="Obit">{{cite web |title=Obituary - David Edmund Caro |publisher= Obituaries Australia |url=https://oa.anu.edu.au/obituary/caro-david-edmund-13919 |access-date=23 October 2025}}</ref>

After the war ended, Caro's RAAF appointment was terminated on 17 January 1946,<ref name="NAA"/> and he returned to his studies at the University of Melbourne, graduating with his [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1946.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article204948523 |title=Prominent Sportsmen Get University Degrees |newspaper=[[The Age]] |issue=28,600 |location=Victoria, Australia |date=23 December 1946 |access-date=24 October 2025 |page=4 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> He them embarked on a [[Master of Science]] degree under the tutelage of [[Philip Law]], who later became the director of the [[Australian National Antarctic Research Expeditions]] from 1949 to 1966. Caro used his electronic skills to build a spectrometer for measuring the cosmic rays in Antarctica, field-testing it on [[Mount Hotham]].<ref name="Obit"/><ref name="e1851">{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article189463599 |title=Scholarships for Scientific Investigations |newspaper=[[The Age]] |issue=29396 |location=Victoria, Australia |date=15 July 1949 |access-date=24 October 2025 |page=2 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |magazine= Australian Antarctic Magazine |issue=18 |year=2010 |title=Vale: Phillip Garth Law AC, CBE, 1912–2010 |url=https://www.antarctica.gov.au/magazine/issue-18-2010/vale/vale-phillip-garth-law-ac-cbe-1912-2010/ |access-date=23 October 2025}}</ref> He was awarded his Master of Science in 1949,<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article22724427 |title=Degrees Conferred on 400 Graduates |newspaper=[[The Argus (Melbourne)]] |issue=32,025 |location=Victoria, Australia |date=25 April 1949 |access-date=24 October 2025 |page=12 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> and was awarded an [[1851 Research Fellowship]] to study in the UK.<ref name="e1851" /><ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article22764733 |title=Melbourne Wins Science Double |newspaper=[[The Argus (Melbourne)]] |issue=32,095 |location=Victoria, Australia |date=15 July 1949 |access-date=23 October 2025 |page=6 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> He went to the [[University of Birmingham]], where he assisted the expatriate Australian professor of physics, [[Mark Oliphant]], in the construction of the Birmingham proton [[synchrotron]].<ref name="Obit"/> He wrote his 1951 [[Doctor of Philosophy]] thesis on "Some aspects of the radio frequency system of the Birmingham proton synchroton".<ref>{{cite thesis |first=David Edmund |last=Caro |title=Some aspects of the radio frequency system of the Birmingham proton synchroton |degree=PhD |publisher=University of Birmingham |url=https://birmingham.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/44BIR_INST/jmfpgg/alma990032808620204871 |access-date=23 October 2025 }}</ref>

==University of Melbourne==
Caro returned to the University of Melbourne, where he was appointed a [[lecturer]] in 1952, [[senior lecturer]] in 1954 and [[reader (academic rank)|reader]] in 1958.<ref name="Eoas">{{cite encyclopedia |entry=Caro, David Edmund - Person |title= Encyclopedia of Australian Science and Innovation |url=https://www.eoas.info/biogs/P004099b.htm |access-date=24 October 2025}}</ref> On 27 February 1954, he married Fiona MacLeod, the younger daughter of Lieutenant Colonel T. B. Macleod, of [[Richmond, Tasmania]], in a ceremony at [[St David's Cathedral, Hobart|St David's Cathedral]] in Hobart officiated by [[Percy Fewtrell]], the [[Dean of Hobart]].<ref name="Wedding">{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article27200128 |title=Page Wears Family Tartan for Colourful Wedding |newspaper=[[The Mercury (Hobart)|The Mercury]] |volume=CLXXIV |issue=25,955 |location=Tasmania, Australia |date=1 March 1954 |access-date=23 October 2025 |page=8 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> They had two children, Richard and Catriona. With research student John Rouse, Caro built a variable-energy [[cyclotron]] at the University of Melbourne, the first of its kind. He commenced the design in June 1953 and construction began in 1954. The machine provided generations of research students with experience in nuclear physics but Caro made little use of it himself; for him the challenge was in building the machine rather than in using it for experiments.<ref name="Obit"/><ref name="Physics">{{cite web |title=History of the School of Physics |date= 19 May 2025 |publisher= The University of Melbourne |url=https://physics.unimelb.edu.au/about/history |access-date=24 October 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=D.E. |last1=Caro |first2=L.H. |last2=Martin |first3=J.L. |author-link2=Leslie H. Martin |last3=Rouse |title=The Melbourne University Variable Energy Cyclotron |journal=Nuclear Instruments and Methods |volume=10 |year=1961 |pages=249–258 |issn=0029-554X |doi=10.1016/S0029-554X(61)80116-X |bibcode=1961NucIM..10..249C }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=D.E. |last1=Caro |first2=J.L. |last2=Rouse |title=A Variable Energy Cyclotron Free |journal=Australian Journal of Physics |date=1955 |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=306–309 |doi=10.1071/PH550306 }}</ref>

Appointed professor of experimental physics and head of the physics department in 1961, Caro overhauled the physics curriculum. Construction of a new physics building was initiated. Opened in 1974, it now bears Caro's name. The physics department's high energy research group conducted experiments at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] in the United States that generated hundreds of thousands of [[bubble chamber]] images. Seeking a way to automate their processing, Caro learned to program computers. After he became deputy vice chancellor in 1972, he computerised the university's administrative systems. He also overhauled the distribution of funds, replacing the old arbitrary mechanisms with a more transparent procedure.<ref name="Obit"/>

==University of Tasmania==
In 1978, Caro became the [[vice-chancellor]] of the [[University of Tasmania]] in Hobart. In this capacity he had to navigate the merger of the university with the Tasmanian College of Advanced Education in [[Launceston, Tasmania|Launceston]]. As deputy vice chancellor at the University of Melbourne he had been concerned at the lack of an adequate staff [[superannuation]] scheme, which he considered an obstacle to good staff relations, and had established a scheme based on both employer and employee contributions. As vice-chancellor of the University of Tasmania he pushed for the creation of a national scheme along these lines. This was established in 1982. The University of Tasmania was the first institution to join the new scheme, and Caro served as the chairman of [[UniSuper]] from 1983 to 1993. By 1995, the scheme held $3 billion in investments.<ref name="Obit"/><ref>{{cite report |first=Lynn |last=Beaton |title=UniSuper Historical Review |url=https://www.marxists.org/subject/women/authors/beaton/2001/unisuper-history.pdf |access-date=25 October 2025 }}</ref>

Another of Caro's interests was Antarctic research. He became the chairman of Antarctic Research Policy Advisory Committee in 1979 and oversaw Australia's current Antarctic program. The committee promoted greater involvement in Antarctic research. A series of research grants was established. Annual flights between Australia and its bases in the Antarctic were instituted and the [[icebreaker]] RSV ''[[Aurora Australis (icebreaker)|Aurora Australis]]'' was acquired in 1989. Caro twice travelled to the Antarctic and even paid a brief visit to the South Pole.<ref name="Obit"/><ref>{{cite web |title=RSV ''Aurora Australis'' 1989–2020 — Australian Antarctic Program |website=www.antarctica.gov.au |date=25 January 2017 |url=https://www.antarctica.gov.au/about-antarctica/history/transportation/shipping/aurora-australis/ |access-date=25 October 2025}}</ref>

==Vice-chancellor==
Caro returned to the University of Melbourne in 1982, this time as vice-chancellor. He was known for his support of centralized services such as the Computer Centre and the University Library, which was boosted with additional acquisitions and funding. He retired in 1987 but the following year he oversaw the merger of the Darwin Institute of Technology with the University College of the Northern Territory to form the University of the Northern Territory, which later became [[Charles Darwin University]]. Caro briefly served as interim vice-chancellor of the new university until a permanent vice-chancellor could be appointed. He also served on the council of the newly-formed [[University of South Australia]] and [[University of Ballarat]], as a director of the [[Melbourne Business School]], and as president of the [[Victorian College of the Arts]]. He was [[chancellor]] of the University of Ballarat from 1995 to 2008.<ref name="Obit"/><ref name="Eoas" /><ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article120860486 |title=Unis responsible for research validity |newspaper=[[The Canberra Times]] |volume=64 |issue=19,763 |location=Australian Capital Territory, Australia |date=17 November 1989 |access-date=25 October 2025 |page=2 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref>

The University of Melbourne awarded Caro an honorary [[Doctor of Laws]] degree in 1978 and a [[Doctor of Science]] degree in 1987.<ref name="Eoas" /> The University of Tasmania also awarded him an honorary Doctor of Laws degree in 1982.<ref>{{cite web |title=Honorary graduates by surname |publisher= University of Tasmania |url=https://www.utas.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0010/1666423/Honorary-Graduates-History-list-CURRENT.pdf |access-date=25 October 2025 }}</ref> He was appointed an [[Officer of the Order of the British Empire]] in the [[1977 New Year Honours]] and an [[Officer of the Order of Australia]] in the [[1986 Australia Day Honours]].<ref>{{London Gazette |date=30 December 1976 |issue=47102 |supp=1 |page=21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=David Edmund Caro |publisher=Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1107509 |access-date=25 October 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=David Edmund Caro |publisher=Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/881193 |access-date=25 October 2025}}</ref>

Caro died in Melbourne on 15 August 2011.<ref name="Obit"/><ref name="Eoas" /> A funeral service was held at Saint John's Anglican Church in [[Toorak]] and his remains were cremated.<ref>{{cite web |title=David Caro Obituary (2011) |publisher= Legacy Remembers |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/legacyremembers/david-caro-obituary?id=41734716 |access-date=25 October 2025}}</ref> His papers are held by the University of Melbourne.<ref>{{cite web |title=[1987.0040] Papers of David Edmund Caro |publisher= University of Melbourne Archives |url=https://archives.library.unimelb.edu.au/nodes/view/68327 |access-date=25 October 2025}}</ref>
